title: Carved sycamore serving spoon, long-handled
subtitle: Green-sycamore serving spoon with a shallow oval bowl
excerpt: A long-handled serving spoon in green sycamore. Axe to knife shaping, hook-knife bowl hollow, raw-linseed cure. At 36 cm handle length it fits a deep salad bowl or soup pot and stays food-safe after the two-week oil cure.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the axe-to-knife blank progression; Newey and Drage Practical Carpentry and Joinery for the green-wood sourcing notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools and shrinks slightly as it dries.
A short length of round or split timber, ready to be worked into a blank.
The rough-shaped piece of wood from which the finished item is carved.
A leather strap charged with abrasive compound, used to maintain a sharp edge between honings. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving.

content.text: A long-handled serving spoon in
green wood

sycamore takes an afternoon of bench work and leaves you with a tool that fits a deep salad bowl or a large pot without scalding your wrist. The bowl is shallow and wide, sized for serving rather than stirring. This is a beginner project that moves through the same axe-to-knife sequence used for eating spoons, but on a longer
blank
and with a shallower bowl.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one. The dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
Wood
This project wants
green wood
. Sycamore is the first choice: it carves cleanly in the green state, takes a smooth surface from the knife, and dries food-safe pale. The long handle means the
billet

needs to be 40 cm long and at least 8 cm across at the widest point. Source from a tree-surgeon's off-cuts, coppice waste, or windfall. Birch works as an alternative; it is marginally harder than sycamore green but dries equally food-safe. Lime carves more easily than either but is softer in service.
Split the log section radially to get a quarter-section. The spoon handle sits on the outer face, the bowl end toward the pith. This keeps the grain running the full length of the handle.
Tools
Carving axe: for roughing the blank shape.
Sloyd knife: for all profiling and refining cuts.
Hook knife, large radius: for the bowl hollow.
Leather strop charged with compound: strop every fifteen minutes.
Waterstone, 1000 grit (optional): for re-establishing an edge if the knife has chipped.
Raw linseed oil: food-safe finish. Cure time is two weeks.
Workspace
A low stool or a carving stump at knee height. The axe work wants outdoor space or a swept floor. A chopping block at thigh height steadies the billet during the axe stage. Bring the
strop
to within arm's reach before you pick up the knife.
Method
Step 1: Draw the profile

Mark the spoon profile on the flat face of the split section. The bowl is 10 cm long and 7 cm wide at the widest point. The handle is 26 cm long and tapers from 3 cm at the bowl shoulder to 1.5 cm at the tip. Mark the depth of the bowl on the side: 1.5 cm deep at the centre.
Step 2: Axe the blank

Use the carving axe to remove waste outside the profile line. Work from the tip of the handle toward the bowl shoulder, keeping the axe swing away from the body. The grain runs from handle tip toward the bowl, so axe cuts toward the handle tip go with the grain. Cuts toward the bowl shoulder can lift and split if the grain rises at the transition; switch to the knife when you get within 5 mm of the line.
Step 3: Profile with the sloyd knife
Take the
blank

in your non-knife hand with a four-finger grip on the work. Use the push cut to refine the handle sides and the transition into the bowl shoulder. The blade travels away from the body, driven by the forearm. At the bowl shoulder, where the grain direction shifts, use a
stop cut
across the grain before making the side cuts, to prevent the blade pulling past the intended boundary.
Step 4: Hollow the bowl

Use the large hook knife to hollow the bowl. Grip the spoon bowl-up in the four-finger grip. The hook knife works in the opposite direction to the sloyd: it cuts on the pull toward you. This is not a pull cut in the safety-sense; the hook knife's curved blade means the cutting arc stays inside the bowl and never travels toward any body part. Take light curving cuts, rotating the spoon so each cut follows the oval of the bowl. Work from the centre outward. The bowl depth is 1.5 cm at the deepest point. Walls should be 5 to 7 mm thick at the rim.
Strop the hook knife every fifteen minutes. The hook knife edge dulls faster than the sloyd knife because it works against the grain on most cuts.
Step 5: Back of the bowl

Turn the spoon over. Use the sloyd knife with a push cut to refine the underside of the bowl into a smooth dome. The transition from handle to bowl back is the test cut: the grain runs one way across the bowl shoulder on one side, and the other way on the other side. Try a push cut; if the wood lifts and tears, reverse direction. One side of the bowl back will be going with the grain; the other will be going against it. Work from the rim toward the centre on each side so both cuts go with the grain.
Step 6: Handle shaping

Round the handle off the square with a push cut. The cross-section at mid-handle should be an oval: slightly taller than wide. The tip can be flat, domed, or pointed. For a serving spoon the flat tip is practical: it rests steady on a plate rim. Use a
pull cut
for the final refinement of the handle tip, with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc not reaching the body.
Finishing

Leave the freshly carved spoon to dry in a warm room for one week before oiling. If you oil it before drying, the oil seals the surface and the moisture inside the wood cannot escape evenly; this increases the risk of cracking.

Once dry, apply raw linseed oil liberally with a cloth. Let it soak in for one hour, then wipe off the surplus. Repeat the application after 24 hours, then leave for two weeks before food contact. Raw linseed oil is a drying oil: it hardens through oxidation, not evaporation. The two-week cure is not negotiable for food-safe use.
Variations
Birch in place of sycamore. Birch dries slightly harder and takes a good finish from the knife.
Shorten the handle to 20 cm for a pasta-serving spoon or a sauce ladle.
Left-handed version: reverse the bowl hollow direction and orientate the hook knife for the left-hand grip.
Care

Wash by hand with warm soapy water immediately after use. Dry with a cloth and leave standing or hanging, not flat on a wet surface. Re-oil with raw linseed oil or board butter every three to four months or when the wood looks dry. Never soak in water and never put in a dishwasher.

attrs.symptom: The bowl walls are thin on one side
attrs.cause: The hook knife drifted off the oval track, removing too much from one side.
attrs.fix: Mark the oval centre line on the bowl face with a pencil before hollowing. Keep the knife on the line on each pass.

attrs.symptom: The handle has tear-out near the bowl shoulder
attrs.cause: The sloyd knife cut against the grain at the transition point.
attrs.fix: Use a stop cut across the grain first, then approach from the handle side with short push cuts so the blade is always travelling into supported wood.

attrs.symptom: The spoon cracked down the handle during drying
attrs.cause: The walls dried unevenly, or the spoon was left in direct sunlight or near a heat source.
attrs.fix: Dry the next spoon slowly, away from direct heat, at room temperature. Even wall thickness helps; walls that vary from 3 mm to 10 mm in the same spoon dry at different rates and crack at the thin points.

attrs.symptom: The knife is not cutting: it is compressing the wood
attrs.fix: Strop the knife and test again. If it still will not cut, hone on the 1000-grit waterstone.
